transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-22
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Liam Carter (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marta Ruiz (Arbor Head of AI), Ben Kwan (Arbor Platform Eng), Aisha Malik (Arbor Security PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Arbor Insurance is evaluating Redwood for a pilot to replace an internal OpenAI-compatible proxy they run for claim summarization and structured extraction. Main concerns: latency at peak concurrency, cost per token, SSO/KMS, and ability to return validated JSON (structured output) and function/tool calling for downstream RPA. Agreed next step: Redwood will run synthetic benchmarks against Arbor prompts and provide pilot proposal + security docs.

Topics covered:
- Success criteria and acceptance metrics
- Workload sizing: tokens, concurrency, QPS
- Benchmark plan: synthetic + replay tests
- Integration surface: OpenAI-compatible endpoints, SDKs, function/tool calling, structured output (json schemas)
- Deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem)
- Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam Carter: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. Quick intros, we'll keep this focused—Priya will run the technical portion.
[00:12] Marta Ruiz: Hi, Marta here. We're looking to scope a POC to validate Redwood can handle our claim-summarization pipeline and output structured JSON for our downstream rules engine.
[00:22] Ben Kwan: Ben, platform, I'll be doing most of the bench work on our side. Key thing for us is peak-day concurrency, we see sudden spikes during claims events.
[00:33] Aisha Malik: Aisha, security PM. My focus is encryption at rest/in transit, and KMS integration. Also audit logs for regulatory review.
[00:43] Priya Desai: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: define success criteria, go over typical workload (tokens, concurrency), propose a benchmarking plan, and then integration approach — SDKs and OpenAI-compatible endpoints, function calling and structured output.
[00:57] Marta Ruiz: Sounds good. For success criteria, internal stakeholders want: 1) extraction accuracy for the JSON schema > 92% on our eval set, 2) p95 latency under 350 ms for single-turn short summaries, 3) cost per 1k tokens under target — we'll share target numbers, and 4) predictable scaling — no tail latency spikes.
[01:18] Liam Carter: Good, that aligns with what we've seen. For p95 350 ms, is that cold-start inclusive or steady-state?
[01:24] Marta Ruiz: Steady-state ideally. We'll tolerate some cold start but we need graceful degradation and fallback.
[01:30] Priya Desai: Okay noted. On the workload: Ben, can you give us the token distribution and concurrency?
[01:36] Ben Kwan: Typical call is 120–320 tokens input, outputs 50–180 tokens. Average QPS is 12 during normal hours, 160 peak during incident bursts. Concurrency can hit 300 concurrent requests if many claims stream in.
[01:53] Priya Desai: That's helpful. For a POC we should mirror both normal and peak. We'll run two benchmark profiles: 1) steady at 12 QPS for 1 hour, 2) burst test with step ramp to 160 QPS and sustained 10 minutes, plus a concurrency stress to 300 concurrent.
[02:12] Marta Ruiz: We can provide replay logs for two weeks; we'll anonymize before sharing.
[02:18] Ben Kwan: We'll export xff logs and a sample prompt set, including the edge cases we care about.
[02:24] Priya Desai: Great. For benchmarks we'll measure latency p50/p95/p99, token cost, tail errors, and correctness against your labeled set for the structured JSON. We'll also test function-calling flows — e.g., model returns a JSON payload and Redwood invokes a webhook or a tool call.
[02:40] Aisha Malik: On tool calling — we need assurance that callbacks go to our VPC and are authenticated. How does Redwood handle webhooks for Private or Dedicated deployments?
[02:50] Liam Carter: For Redwood Dedicated we can route callbacks through customer-managed networking; for Private (VPC/on-prem) the callbacks can be internal-only. For hosted API we support signed webhooks and mTLS; I'll follow up with the architecture note.
[03:06] Marta Ruiz: Can you confirm SDK support? We currently use an internal OpenAI-compatible wrapper; it'd be easiest if Redwood supports the same OpenAI API surface so we don't refactor much.
[03:16] Priya Desai: Yes — Redwood exposes an OpenAI-compatible REST endpoint and we have official SDKs (Python, Node) with drop-in replace examples. There are small differences in advanced fields for routing and pinning model versions, but generally it's compatible. We'll share an example repo.
[03:31] Ben Kwan: Any limits on function calling or structured output? We rely on model to output JSON that passes a specific schema; sometimes it returns extra fields or malformed JSON. How does Redwood help validate or enforce schema?
[03:44] Priya Desai: Two approaches: 1) Use our structured output feature that can enforce JSON schemas at the runtime layer and reject malformed results, and 2) use post-processing hooks — Redwood Console can run a lightweight validation step and flag regressions. We'll demonstrate both. Note: the structured output enforcement is part of Redwood Optimize features for pilots, but we can enable for POC.
[04:05] Marta Ruiz: That enforcement is critical. Otherwise our rules engine chokes.
[04:09] Liam Carter: We'll enable a strict schema check for the pilot. If the model returns non-conforming output, Redwood can return a specific error code so you can fallback to existing logic.
[04:19] Aisha Malik: About encryption — we need customer-managed keys. Do you integrate with external KMS?
[04:25] Priya Desai: Yes, we support customer-managed KMS (AWS KMS, GCP CMEK, and HSM for Private). For Dedicated we can offer a KMS integration that meets your compliance. We'll attach the KMS architecture doc.
[04:36] Ben Kwan: If we run a functional test that requires tool calling into our internal systems, what's the best approach without exposing prod systems?
[04:45] Priya Desai: For the POC we recommend a staging webhook behind your VPC or a short-lived tunnel with mutual TLS. We can also simulate responses in Redwood Console to validate end-to-end without hitting production.
[04:58] Marta Ruiz: Let's talk timelines — we want a 4-week POC: week 0 prep, week 1 synthetic bench, week 2 replay test + accuracy eval, week 3 pilot tweak + stakeholder review. Is that doable?
[05:11] Liam Carter: Yes, that's a reasonable cadence. Our typical turnaround: bench results in 3–5 business days after we get your prompts/logs. Pilot pricing and environment provisioning may take up to a week (sometimes earlier if Dedicated capacity is requested).
[05:24] Marta Ruiz: For acceptance: if we hit correctness >92% and p95 <350ms on steady workload and no significant error tail at peak, we'll consider it a success. Also need an estimate for unit costs so we can model spend.
[05:37] Priya Desai: We'll include cost modeling based on observed tokens and the recommended quantization/variant. We might suggest a 4-bit quantized variant for cost reduction if latency remains acceptable.
[05:48] Ben Kwan: About caching — does Redwood support KV cache or prefix caching to reduce cost for repetitive prompts?
[05:55] Priya Desai: Yes. Redwood has prefix/KV caching which can reduce token usage significantly for repeated boilerplate. We'll instrument cache hit rates in the Console so you can see savings. Caching is configurable per route.
[06:07] Aisha Malik: Audit logs — we need token-level redaction and retention controls.
[06:12] Liam Carter: Audit logs can be configured with redaction rules and retention policies; for Private we can keep logs in your account. We'll share the audit spec doc.
[06:22] Marta Ruiz: One more thing — integration with our existing OpenAI-compatible wrapper: if Redwood accepts the same API keys and endpoints, we can swap easily. How do we handle model pinning and rollbacks?
[06:33] Priya Desai: Redwood supports model pinning per route and rollouts. You can create a canary with 10% traffic, evaluate metrics in Console, then promote or rollback. We'll walk through the Console controls during the engineers-only kickoff.
[06:47] Ben Kwan: For the synthetic benchmark, what does Redwood need from us?
[06:51] Priya Desai: Ideally: 1) 20–50 canonical prompts covering happy and edge cases, 2) anonymized replay logs (2 weeks), 3) your eval labels for correctness on a sample of ~500 examples. We'll run bench profiles and return a spreadsheet with latency, cost estimates, accuracy, and error breakdown.
[07:07] Marta Ruiz: We'll prepare that. Any blockers from your side for running the benchmarks?
[07:11] Liam Carter: None. We'll need an engineering contact to coordinate keys and routing for the replay harness.
[07:17] Ben Kwan: That'll be me.
[07:19] Aisha Malik: On compliance — are you SOC2 Type II? We need a copy of the report for procurement.
[07:25] Liam Carter: Yes, we are SOC2 Type II. We'll share the cert and the controls mapping. Also will attach the pilot security checklist.
[07:34] Marta Ruiz: Pricing — high level numbers are fine now. For modeling we need cost per 1k input tokens and 1k output tokens for hosted vs dedicated.
[07:44] Priya Desai: We'll provide a cost matrix: hosted (pay-as-you-go), dedicated reserved capacity (monthly commitments) and private (license + infra). For the POC we'll show both hosted and dedicated run-through costs.
[07:58] Ben Kwan: If we hit the success metrics, we likely want Redwood Dedicated for predictable throughput. Is there a minimum commitment?
[08:05] Liam Carter: Typically Reserved Dedicated starts at a monthly commit that covers the baseline throughput you're targeting; we'll propose tiers in the pilot pricing doc.
[08:14] Marta Ruiz: Ok, recapping next steps quickly before we run out of time — Redwood to run synthetic benchmarks, Arbor to send prompt set and replay logs, Redwood to send SOC2 and KMS docs, schedule engineers-only kickoff on Sept 2. Anything else?
[08:29] Priya Desai: We'll also share sample SDK snippets, the structured-output enforcement example, and a spreadsheet template for cost modeling.
[08:38] Aisha Malik: Also please include a short note on webhook auth options and sample mTLS config.
[08:44] Liam Carter: Will do.
[08:46] Marta Ruiz: Great. Thanks everyone.
[08:48] Liam Carter: Thanks, we'll follow up with the links and timeline.

End notes: Links referenced (shared in chat):
- POC benchmark spreadsheet (link): https://redwood.example.com/shared/arb-poc-bench.xlsx
- SOC2 summary + security checklist: https://redwood.example.com/docs/soc2-arb.pdf
- SDK drop-in examples repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/sdk-examples/tree/poc-arbor

Meeting recap (auto):
- Agreed acceptance criteria: correctness >92%, p95 <350ms steady, acceptable cost profile, no significant error tail under peak.
- Redwood action: run synthetic benchmarks and share results + pilot pricing + security docs.
- Arbor action: provide anonymized logs, canonical prompts, and confirm engineering kickoff date.

Timestamp alignment: transcript approximate to 52-minute duration (timestamps approximate).

Transcription notes: occasional word errors present — e.g., Red wood mentioned in one spot, function-calling transcribed as function fulling once.
